model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Othello (Reversi) on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: np.ndarray, opponent: np.ndarray) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move when `policy` is called. - `you` and `opponent` are 8x8 numpy arrays containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid: never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Move coordinates use algebraic notation: columns `a..h` map to `c = 0..7`, rows `1..8` map to `r = 0..7`. For example, `a4` maps to you[3][0] - The game ends when neither player has a legal move (or the board is full). - Objective: finish with more discs than the opponent; ties are draws. # Action / Return Format - Return a move string like `"d3"` (file letter `a..h` + rank `1..8`). - A legal move must place a disc on an empty cell that flips at least one opponent disc in any direction. - Flips occur along any of the 8 directions where the new disc brackets a contiguous line of opponent discs ending in your disc. - If you have no legal moves, return `"pass"`. You may not return `"pass"` if you have legal moves. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning to build a fast Othello engine using bitboards for move generation, alpha-beta search with iterative deepening under a time budget, and an evaluation function combining mobility, corners, stability, and positional weights, switching to exact endgame solving when few empty squares remain.

I'm also making sure the code always returns a legal move by wrapping search in a fallback that picks a simple legal move if anything fails, then working through the bit-shift logic for generating legal moves using masks that exclude wraparound columns for each of the eight directions.

Writing bitboard move generation...

I'm also weighing X-square penalties, mobility and potential mobility, frontier disc penalties, and an approximate stability calculation that iteratively marks discs stable if they're anchored to corners or full lines along each axis.

This gets complicated fast, especially with diagonals of varying lengths. I'm thinking I should simplify by focusing stability checks on rows, columns, and full-board occupancy, and skip a fully rigorous diagonal treatment to keep things tractable in Python.

Estimating Python throughput more concretely: move generation and stability checks likely limit search to a few thousand leaves per second, giving maybe depth 4-5 in midgame, which should be sufficient against simpler baseline opponents.

For popcount I'll use int.bit_count when available, falling back to bin(x).count for older Python. For the endgame, exact solving at 12+ empties may exceed the search budget, so I'll rely on iterative deepening with time control throughout rather than a fixed empties threshold for switching to exact search.

I'm setting a time budget of roughly 0.5 seconds (safely under the 1-second limit), checking elapsed time periodically during search and falling back to the best move from the last completed depth if time runs out. I also need to handle pass situations within the search—when the side to move has no legal moves, either the game ends (if the opponent also can't move) or the turn switches without decrementing depth.

Now I'm defining the evaluation function using corner counts, mobility, potential mobility (empty squares adjacent to opponent discs versus my own), and frontier discs adjacent to empty squares...

I'm assigning weights to each factor: corners are worth the most, then stability, mobility, potential mobility, with frontier discs penalized negatively, plus penalties for x-squares and c-squares near open corners, and a disc-parity term that grows more important as the endgame approaches. I'm also laying out the standard positional weight table, giving high value to corners and edges while heavily penalizing squares adjacent to corners.

Rather than looping over all 64 squares to compute this, I'm switching to a faster bitmask approach -- grouping squares into weight classes (corners, X-squares, C-squares, edges, inner ring) and summing weight times popcount for each mask against my discs, applying the corner-dependent penalties conditionally only when the relevant corner is still empty.

For stability I'm working out full-line detection along all four axes using shifted bitboards with edge masks to prevent wraparound, then precomputing the fixed row, column, and diagonal masks needed to check whether an entire line is occupied.

The stability propagation loop starts with discs that already sit on fully-occupied lines or corners, then iteratively expands the stable set by checking each candidate against combined full-line-or-adjacent-stable masks along all four directions until no new stable discs are found — though I'm now second-guessing whether a disc counts as stable on an axis just because its neighbor in that direction is stable.

I confirm the reasoning holds: if a stable neighbor exists along an axis, flipping that disc would require flipping the neighbor too, which can't happen, so the approximation is sound though incomplete. Now I'm shifting to think about move ordering using static square priority weights.

For deeper nodes (depth ≥ 3) I'll add opponent-mobility-based ordering on top of square weights, since minimizing opponent options tends to correlate with strong moves, though it costs extra move generation at each child. I'll also set up a transposition table keyed by the board state, storing depth, flag, value, and best move, persisting across calls but bounded in size.

Since disc counts only ever increase during a game, cached positions never recur, so I'm clearing the table at the start of each policy call rather than trying to reuse stale entries.

Writing negamax search logic...

For terminal positions I'll score based on disc difference scaled heavily (times 10000) so wins dominate the heuristic evaluation, and I want the weighting toward pure disc count to increase as the endgame approaches with fewer empty squares.

For iterative deepening at the root, I'm going from depth 1 up to 64, saving the best move after each completed depth and catching timeouts, with a conservative ~0.6s budget and checking elapsed time every 64 nodes for fine granularity. Since search depth naturally reaches the terminal state once depth meets empty count, I don't need a special leaner evaluation for deep endgame search — I'll handle numpy-to-bitboard conversion with straightforward loops and add a safety fallback that verifies the chosen move is actually in the legal move list before returning it.

Writing bitboard move generator...

Still writing move-generation logic...

Adding corner and X-square penalties...

I'll use the raw mobility difference rather than normalizing it, since stable discs already account for corner value through the stability weight. I should also make disc count matter less in the early game, favoring flexibility over material there.

For time management, I'll check the deadline every node since the overhead is negligible compared to node processing cost. For move ordering, I'll precompute static square weights and extract moves bit by bit, storing the best move per position in the transposition table for future ordering hints.

At the root, I'll reuse move scores from the previous iterative deepening pass to sort moves before the next iteration, and short-circuit immediately if there's only one legal move available.

For endgame, once few empties remain the search should complete exactly, using disc difference plus empties as the terminal evaluation. I'll cap depth at the number of empties and halt deepening once a full exact search completes, avoiding wasted time on further iterations.

If a deepening iteration takes too long, I can predict it likely won't finish and abort early, though any partial results from an aborted search go unused unless I carefully track which root moves were fully searched before the timeout — using those completed evaluations only if they clearly beat the previous best.

Now I'm setting up the bitboard constants and beginning to write the move generation helper functions...

Finishing the diagonal masks and defining square weights for move ordering, then writing the negamax search with a timeout check, terminal scoring, and depth-limited evaluation fallback.

Now I'm adding transposition table lookups with bound flags, then building an ordered move list that prioritizes squares by static weight and opponent mobility reduction for deeper searches, with the transposition-table move getting priority in sorting.

Writing the iterative deepening loop...

Now I'm thinking through the choose_move function: resetting the transposition table and node counters, setting the deadline, generating root moves, and ordering them by square weight for the first pass. I'm structuring the depth-increasing loop where each iteration runs negamax on ordered moves and tracks the best score, catching a timeout exception so the search can gracefully fall back to the best move found so far.

If at least one move finished searching before a timeout, I'll trust that partial result even though deeper analysis might reveal it wasn't optimal—there's no better alternative available. After each completed depth, I reorder moves by their scores for better pruning next iteration, and stop once depth reaches the number of empty squares since the search becomes exact at that point. I'm weighing whether to add an early-exit heuristic based on elapsed time fraction, but decide to let the timeout mechanism handle it naturally rather than adding extra prediction logic, while also reconsidering how tight to set the time budget given CPU variance in the arena's one-second limit.

I'm settling on a 0.55 second search budget to leave margin for timeout-check granularity and move-ordering overhead. I'm also confirming that pass moves in the search don't need special TT handling since they return before storage, and that periodic time checks every 32 nodes keep overhead low.

Writing stability detection logic...

Now I'm working through evaluation weight tuning, roughly balancing corner value, mobility, potential moves, frontier discs, stable discs, and dangerous X/C-squares, with disc-difference weight scaling up as the endgame approaches.

Adding a small edge-ownership bonus, then writing helper code to convert numpy board arrays into bitboards, format square indices into standard move notation, and implement a straightforward fallback legal-move generator that scans the board directly for flankable opponent lines instead of using bitboard tricks.

I'm now sketching the top-level policy function that wraps everything in a try/except: convert boards to bitboards, pick a move with the search, verify legality, and fall back to the simple array-based move generator if anything fails or times out, returning "pass" when no legal moves exist. I'm also double-checking that numpy integer truthiness works fine in these comparisons, and reconsidering the evaluation weights—corner value around 100, X-square penalty around -50, mobility difference contributing roughly 30 points for a 5-move edge—as reasonable ordering heuristics for deeper search.

Now I'm unrolling the directional move generation manually for speed, writing out each of the eight shift directions as separate blocks rather than a loop.

Writing directional shift blocks...

Then I want to consolidate into two compact loops over the four shift/mask pairs for each direction (left-shift and right-shift groups) since that's cleaner while still fast, and I'll mirror the same pattern for make_move. I also need to make sure pass handling works correctly when gen_moves returns zero, that terminal scoring triggers when both sides have no moves, and that the iterative deepening loop caps depth at the number of empty squares since passes don't consume depth. Now I'm ready to write out the complete file.
